title: Introducing The Ultimate Retrieval Tool Date Published: June 4, 2026 Original URL: https://eedi.substack.com
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton announces The Ultimate Retrieval Tool, a free mathematics quiz generator designed to address six specific pedagogical problems that he argues no existing tool solves: quiz regeneration via a shareable code, fixed 4- or 10-question formats that fit exactly on one side of A4, blocked or interleaved topic selection, geometry diagram generation, per-question regeneration with a single click, and follow-up quiz generation across a whole quiz. The article is structured as a rationale for each of the six design decisions, explaining the pedagogical reasoning behind choices like limiting to 4 or 10 questions (4 for a retrieval Do Now, 10 for a weekly low-stakes quiz), so readers understand not just what the tool does but why. A persistent frustration Barton addresses is the problem of quiz ephemerality: tools that generate good quizzes cannot reproduce them, making it impossible to project answers after printing, share a quiz with a colleague, or offer students a homework version of the same content. The interleaving feature reflects decades of research on desirable difficulties: mixed-topic quizzes force students to determine which method a question requires, not just execute a known procedure — which is what examinations demand but what most classroom practice never rehearses. The geometry diagram capability represents a significant technical advance: AI can now render diagrams reliably, expanding retrieval practice beyond arithmetic and algebra to angle facts, statistical diagrams, trigonometry, and circle theorems. Four practical use cases are described: the mixed-topic Do Now, the weekly low-stakes quiz, the in-lesson follow-up using the regeneration button after explanation, and student self-quizzing at home using the shareable code.
points: The quiz regeneration problem is one of Barton's most specific and useful observations: building a quiz outside the lesson and then being unable to reproduce it in the lesson — or share it with colleagues — is a genuine friction point that renders much off-site planning labor functionally useless.

The fixed 4/10 question format is a deliberate constraint that produces a benefit: by sacrificing flexibility, the tool guarantees that print formatting works reliably every time, solving a mundane but real problem that teachers encounter repeatedly with generative tools.

Interleaving in the tool is not just topic switching but demands the cognitive skill that examinations actually test: identifying which method to apply, not just applying a given method — a distinction that blocked practice systematically fails to develop.

The in-lesson regeneration button creates a formative assessment loop: explain a concept, click for a new question on the same skill, have students answer on mini-whiteboards, and gain evidence about whether the explanation actually landed rather than accepting 'Does that make sense?' as feedback.

The follow-up quiz function supports spaced practice protocols: run the same topics as Do Nows across a week, generate five versions in seconds, or set a Thursday quiz for Friday feedback and provide a fresh version Monday to measure what has actually transferred.
quotes: The frustrating thing about most generators is that you build something good and then cannot get it back. A quiz you made at the weekend is no use if you cannot regenerate it on Monday morning. And a quiz you built before the lesson and printed off is not much use if you can't then access it in the lesson to call up all the answers and worked solutions.

Four is ideal for a retrieval Do Now. Ten is ideal for a weekly Low-Stakes Quiz. And because the number is fixed, I can guarantee the printing works. A ten-question quiz fits exactly on one side of A4. A four-question quiz fits two to a side. No awkward half-pages, no font shrinking question by question.

Block practice tells them which skill to use. Interleaving makes them choose. Mixing topics forces students to do the thing exams demand and classrooms rarely rehearse: working out which method a question is even asking for.

In the lesson, your students struggle with a question, you offer an explanation, you click for a follow-up, which students answer on mini-whiteboards. Now you have evidence about whether your explanation actually landed, instead of a hopeful 'Does that make sense?'

Once a quiz is locked in, one button builds a follow-up of the entire quiz: the same skills, in the same order, with fresh numbers throughout. So if you run the same topics across a week of Do Nows, you can generate five versions in seconds.
Set a low-stakes quiz on Thursday, let students revise it over the weekend, and hand them a fresh version on Monday. Same skills, new questions, and a clean read on what has actually stuck.
